title: Certificates of Deposit: Parties to Certificate Bookings and When Bookings Take Effect
content:
Several kinds of booking can concern one of Piedmont Crescent Bank's Certificates of Deposit once its grace period has run out: some the bank owes on its own records, one the owner makes with the owner's own money. This page explains who carries out each kind and how a booking takes effect.

## Bank-side bookings

The agent carries out the bookings the bank owes on its own records. Among those that can arise on a certificate at this stage of its life are:

- a credit to the ledger that cancels a charge the certificate terms did not permit, which raises the principal by that charge;
- a new entry for a standing maturity instruction that the bank can no longer carry out, together with the payout account that goes with it;
- the booking of a certificate's next term, which returns it to active status and fixes the term's dates, rate and bonus markers.

## The owner's booking

Placing new money into a certificate is the owner's own act. The agent makes the transfer available, and the customer themselves carries it out; it is the owner moving the owner's money, not the owner approving something the agent has done.

## How bookings take effect

Every one of these bookings is made directly in the bank's own records and counts from the instant it is made. Nothing in them depends on a delivery, a clearing of funds or the lapse of any period.

A certificate's record has separate parts. The ledger and the principal it produces are one; the standing instructions and the payout account are another; the status, the term dates, the rate and the bonus markers form a third. A booking that changes one part leaves the figures held in the other parts exactly as they were.

The status shown on the record is the status that the in-term add-on terms and the customer-wide principal ceiling each read when money is placed into the certificate.
